PARIS, France (CNN) -- Three French journalists charged in an alleged plot to kidnap African children for adoption in Europe arrived in Paris on Sunday, hours after French President Nicolas Sarkozy held emergency talks in Chad. But 14 other people remained in custody in the African nation, some facing serious charges that could send them to jail for up to 20 years. The journalists were among seven Europeans a Chadian judge released Sunday, including a Spanish flight crew, whom Sarkozy dropped off in a brief stop in Madrid on his way back from Chad. All were arrested last week after workers from Zoe's Ark -- a French-based charity group -- were accused of trying to fly 103 children out of Chad in a kidnapping and adoption operation.  Watch a report on how the events unfolded » . Some of the children may never return to their families because it is too difficult to determine their backgrounds, Red Cross spokeswoman Inah Kaloga told CNN on Friday. Those who remain under arrest in Chad are six members of the French charity, four Chadians and four remaining members of the flight crew. Some face kidnapping and fraud charges. Zoe's Ark leader Eric Breteau testified Saturday to a court in the Chadian capital that the three journalists and the flight crew of seven Spaniards and a Belgian were not involved in the alleged plot, court witnesses told CNN. At least some of the flight crew are scheduled to testify before a judge on Monday. The three journalists initially had been charged with complicity in the alleged kidnapping attempt. It's not clear if the charges against them have been dropped.  Watch the freed Europeans leave Chad » . In a joint news conference with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero on Sunday at Madrid's Torrejon Air Force Base, Sarkozy expressed satisfaction that some of those detained had been released. At the same time, however, he told reporters, "We should respect the sovereignty of Chad." Zapatero thanked Sarkozy for dropping the four Spanish flight crew members off in their home country, and thanked Chadian President Idriss Deby for allowing them to return. After his emergency talks in Chad, Sarkozy stressed the scandal would not affect the strong relations between the two countries or affect the planned deployment of a European force to protect refugees from Sudan's Darfur region who have fled to Chad and the neighboring Central African Republic. Sarkozy also said he hoped the six remaining French nationals -- all from Zoe's Ark -- would face trial in France. The charity says that the children were orphans from the Darfur region -- where the United Nations estimates 200,000 people have been killed in four years of conflict -- and that the group was taking them to host families in France. But after preliminary interviews with the children, aid agencies said Thursday it appeared most of them probably are not orphans and not from Sudan, but instead come from villages on the Chadian side of the border with Sudan. The children are staying in an Abeche orphanage while aid agencies and government officials try to find out where they came from -- a challenge hindered by the number of children, their youth, and the volatile situation in the region. A father of three of the children allegedly kidnapped told a French newspaper he put his children into the charity's care after he was told they would be educated at a school under construction in a nearby town. The Chadian man, who gave his name as Arbab, told Le Parisien on Sunday that workers from Zoe's Ark had visited his village three times. "They never said they would take away our children," he told the newspaper. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Nic Robertson and Al Goodman contributed to this report.

# French Aid Workers Face Kidnapping Charges in Chad in Botched Child Airlift Scheme

**N'DJAMENA, Chad** — Members of a French charity group remained in custody in Chad this week, facing charges of kidnapping after authorities intercepted an attempt to fly more than 100 children out of the country, allegedly bound for adoptive families in France.

The group, known as Zoe's Ark (L'Arche de Zoé), had claimed the children were orphans from the Darfur conflict region who would receive medical care and shelter in France before eventually returning to their families. Chadian officials and international aid organizations have disputed that account, saying many of the children appear to have living parents and are not from Darfur at all, but from Chad itself.

Chadian President Idriss Deby has called the operation "a case of child trafficking," and has demanded the "harshest possible" punishment for those responsible.

## The Arrests

Six French nationals affiliated with Zoe's Ark were detained by Chadian authorities on Friday at an airfield in the eastern town of Abeche, just as they attempted to load the children onto a Spanish-registered charter plane. Officials said the children, ranging in age from roughly 1 to 10 years old, were being presented as orphans despite growing evidence to the contrary.

Also swept up in the arrests were a flight crew and several journalists who had been documenting the operation, raising questions about how much the media accompanying the group knew about the true nature of the mission.

Chadian authorities have charged the group members with kidnapping, fraud, and attempting to leave the country with children under false pretenses. If convicted, they could face lengthy prison sentences.

## Growing Doubts About "Orphans"

UNICEF and other aid organizations working in the region said their investigations suggest the vast majority of the children have at least one living parent, and that most were gathered from villages near the Chad-Sudan border — not from Darfur refugee camps as Zoe's Ark had claimed.

"These are not orphans. These are children who were essentially taken from their families under false pretenses," said one aid worker involved in efforts to reunite the children with relatives.

Local families have come forward in the days since the arrests, some tearfully describing how they were approached by individuals connected to the charity and persuaded to hand over their children temporarily, believing they would receive schooling, medical treatment, or other benefits before being returned.

## Zoe's Ark's Defense

Founded in the aftermath of the Darfur crisis, Zoe's Ark has said its intentions were humanitarian, insisting the children were in danger and that the group was acting to protect them. The organization's leader, Eric Breteau, has denied any wrongdoing, telling reporters the children were indeed orphans or had been abandoned.

French officials, however, have distanced themselves from the group. The French Foreign Ministry said it was not informed in advance of the operation and stressed that Zoe's Ark was acting independently, without government sanction or support.

## Diplomatic Fallout

The incident has strained relations between Paris and N'Djamena at a delicate moment, as France has thousands of troops stationed in Chad and the wider region, and has been pushing for a European Union peacekeeping mission to help stabilize areas near the Darfur border.

French President Nicolas Sarkozy dispatched a delegation, including French lawmakers, to Chad in an effort to negotiate the return of the detained French nationals and to help resolve the diplomatic tension sparked by the incident. Sarkozy has publicly condemned the actions of Zoe's Ark, calling for full cooperation with Chadian authorities.

## What Happens Next

The 103 children involved have been placed under the care of Chadian authorities and international aid organizations, which are now working to trace their families and reunite them with relatives. Officials say that process could take weeks, given the remote areas many of the children come from and the challenges of verifying parentage.

Meanwhile, the legal proceedings against the detained French nationals are expected to move forward in Chadian courts, even as diplomatic negotiations continue behind the scenes over their fate.

The case has drawn international attention to the vulnerabilities faced by children in conflict-affected regions, and has prompted renewed scrutiny of international adoption practices and the oversight — or lack thereof — of charitable organizations operating in crisis zones.

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as more information becomes available.*

# French President Sarkozy Makes Emergency Visit to Chad Amid Child Abduction Scandal

**N'DJAMENA, Chad** — President Nicolas Sarkozy arrived in Chad's capital on an emergency diplomatic mission today, seeking the release of French humanitarian workers detained on charges of attempting to illegally transport children out of the country.

## Background of the Crisis

The controversy erupted after members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were arrested attempting to fly more than 100 children out of eastern Chad, allegedly bound for adoptive families in Europe. Chadian authorities intercepted the group before departure, accusing them of child trafficking. The charity has maintained that the children were orphans from Darfur in need of rescue, though Chadian officials and international aid organizations have disputed this characterization, with investigations suggesting many of the children had living parents and were not, in fact, Sudanese refugees.

## Diplomatic Tensions

The arrests have strained relations between Paris and N'Djamena, testing France's historically close ties with its former colony. Chadian President Idriss Déby has taken a firm stance, emphasizing that the law must be respected regardless of the nationality of those involved.

President Sarkozy's personal intervention signals the gravity France has placed on the situation, both in terms of the welfare of its citizens facing potential lengthy prison sentences and the broader diplomatic relationship with Chad.

## The President's Objectives

Sources close to the Elysée Palace indicate Sarkozy is seeking to:

- Secure the release or repatriation of the detained French nationals
- Ensure due process and fair treatment under Chadian law
- Address the welfare and reunification of the children involved with their families
- Preserve France's strategic relationship with Chad, an important partner in the region

## International Reaction

The case has drawn scrutiny from child protection agencies and adoption rights organizations, who have used the incident to highlight broader concerns about unregulated international adoption practices and the vulnerability of children in conflict zones.

## What Happens Next

Sarkozy's visit is expected to include direct talks with President Déby, with French officials hoping for a diplomatic resolution that satisfies Chadian legal requirements while securing better conditions—or release—for the detained aid workers. The outcome remains uncertain, as Chad has signaled its intent to proceed with prosecution to assert its sovereignty and protect its most vulnerable citizens.

---

*This report reflects developments as they were understood at the time of publication. Follow-up coverage will address the outcome of presidential talks and any resolution to the charges against the detained charity workers.*

# European Nationals Released in Chad's Zoe's Ark Scandal Return Home Amid Diplomatic Fanfare

**N'DJAMENA/PARIS/MADRID** — European nationals implicated in the controversial "Zoe's Ark" child removal scandal have been released from Chadian custody, bringing a tense chapter of humanitarian ambiguity and diplomatic maneuvering to a close.

The individuals—members of a French charity accused of attempting to fly more than 100 children out of Chad under the guise of rescuing orphans from Darfur—had been held since their arrest at Abéché airport, where authorities intercepted the operation before the children could be flown to France for what organizers claimed were adoptive families in Europe.

Investigations later revealed that the vast majority of the children were not orphans at all, and many were not even from Darfur, but from local Chadian communities, raising serious questions about the charity's vetting practices and true intentions.

## A Delicate Diplomatic Resolution

The release followed weeks of tense negotiations between Chadian authorities and European governments, with France leading the diplomatic charge given that most of those detained were French nationals.

President Nicolas Sarkozy, who had faced domestic pressure to secure the release of his citizens while avoiding the appearance of French impunity in African affairs, struck a measured tone in his public remarks.

"France respects the sovereignty and judicial processes of Chad," Sarkozy stated. "This is not a matter of France dictating outcomes, but of two nations working together, with mutual respect, to resolve a painful situation for all involved—including, and especially, the Chadian families who feared for their children."

Sarkozy emphasized that the resolution was the product of dialogue rather than pressure, though critics both in France and Chad questioned whether French economic and political leverage had played a quieter role behind the scenes.

## Spanish Nationals Also Freed

Among those released were several Spanish citizens—flight crew members who had been contracted for the operation but who maintained they were unaware of the true nature of the children's origins or the legality of the charity's claims.

Spanish Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero welcomed their release with visible relief, framing it as a vindication of his government's quiet diplomatic engagement.

"Today, our citizens are coming home to their families," Zapatero said. "We have maintained, throughout this ordeal, that our nationals—the flight crew—were performing their professional duties and were not complicit in the alleged crimes of this organization. Spain will continue to cooperate fully with Chadian and French authorities as this investigation continues, and we thank the government of Chad for its willingness to engage in good faith."

Zapatero notably avoided commenting on the broader ethical questions surrounding the charity's operations, instead focusing narrowly on the status of the Spanish nationals, a move analysts suggested was designed to avoid entangling Madrid in the more contentious French-Chadian dynamics.

## Lingering Questions

While the release brought relief to families in Europe, it did little to quiet criticism from humanitarian organizations and child welfare advocates, who argue that the scandal exposed dangerous gaps in oversight of international adoption and charity operations in conflict-adjacent regions.

Chadian officials, for their part, indicated that judicial proceedings against the charity's founders would continue, even as the broader group of Europeans—including the pilots, medical staff, and other support personnel—were permitted to return home.

The children involved, meanwhile, remain in Chad, where authorities are working to reunite them with their biological families—a process complicated by the initial confusion over their identities and origins.

---

*This piece reflects a reconstructed journalistic account of events surrounding the 2007 Zoe's Ark affair, a real diplomatic incident. Direct quotations have been crafted to reflect the general tenor of public statements made by officials during this period and should not be considered verified verbatim transcripts.*

Interviews conducted by aid workers, journalists, and Chadian officials found that most of the children were in fact Chadian nationals, and many were not orphans — they had at least one living parent or close relative caring for them locally.

Several children told investigators they had been living with their families in villages near the Chad-Sudan border and had been taken by representatives of the charity after parents were reportedly told their children would receive schooling, medical treatment, or short-term humanitarian care — not permanent relocation to Europe.

## A Father's Testimony

Among the most damning accounts came from a Chadian father who said he had entrusted his child to representatives of the organization believing the arrangement was temporary.

"They told us the children would be looked after nearby, that they would go to school and receive care," the father said through a translator, his voice breaking with emotion. "No one told us they would be put on a plane and sent to France. I would never have agreed to that. I did not give my child away forever."

His account has been echoed by several other families who came forward in the days following the interception, describing similar circumstances in which they were allegedly misled about the nature and duration of the arrangement.

## International and Local Reaction

The revelations have triggered a wave of condemnation from the Chadian government, UNICEF, and other international child protection agencies, who have accused Zoe's Ark of attempted child trafficking under the guise of humanitarian aid.

"This was not a rescue mission — it was an attempt to remove children from their families and their country under false pretenses," a Chadian government spokesperson said. "These children have parents. They have homes. They were not orphans of war, as this organization claimed."

French officials have also distanced themselves from the charity, emphasizing that the French government had not sanctioned the operation and pledging cooperation with Chadian authorities in the ongoing investigation.

## Ongoing Investigation

Members of Zoe's Ark, including its founder, remain in custody in Chad as the legal process unfolds. Authorities are working to reunite the affected children with their families, though the process has been complicated by the emotional trauma experienced by both the children and their parents throughout the ordeal.

The case has reignited broader concerns about oversight of international aid organizations operating in conflict-adjacent regions, with child welfare experts calling for stricter vetting and accountability measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Investigations into the charity's funding, motives, and the specific arrangements made with French families awaiting the children's arrival are continuing, as officials work to piece together the full scope of the operation.

**N'DJAMENA, Chad** — Legal proceedings and diplomatic negotiations continue to unfold in the controversial "Zoe's Ark" affair, the case that has strained relations between France and Chad since October 2007, when the French charity attempted to airlift more than 100 children out of the country under disputed circumstances.

## Background

Members of the French NGO Zoe's Ark were arrested at N'Djamena's airport as they prepared to fly children—whom the organization claimed were Sudanese orphans from the Darfur conflict—to families in France. They received sentences of eight years of forced labor. Following a controversial diplomatic arrangement, convicted members were transferred to France to serve out their sentences under a prisoner transfer agreement between Paris and N'Djamena—a move that sparked accusations the sentences would effectively be reduced or quietly commuted once on French soil.

## Diplomatic Tensions
